To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

most patients in our sample who were eligible for RCTs were eligible for at least one published study and that a substantial number of patients who did not match at least two RCTs for their primary diagnoses did so because they did not meet minimum severity or remission criteria or were being treated with an antidepressant.
most of the patients in this sample who had primary psychiatric diagnoses represented in the randomized controlled trial (RCT) literature were eligible for at least one RCT.
the vast majority of patients in our sample who had primary psychiatric diagnoses represented in the randomized controlled trial (RCT) literature were eligible for at least one RCT.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the generalizability of the psychotherapy research literature to patients in the community.
the generalizability of RCTs of psychotherapy to a sample of nonrandomized patients.
the generalizability of published randomized controlled trials to patients who are seen by clinicians in outpatient mental health settings.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
RCTs of psychotherapy are not a perfect match for patients in routine clinical care.
the literature of RCTs of psychotherapy is not a good generalizable model for the patients who present to outpatient psychotherapy clinics.
the RCT literature can be generalized to nonrandomized outpatients, but the generalizability depends on the characteristics of the patients and the characteristics of the RCTs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the majority of patients in the sample would be eligible for at least one published psychotherapy trial.
the majority of patients in the study were eligible for at least one of the RCTs.
the published RCT literature is generalizable to a large number of outpatients with common psychiatric conditions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the vast majority of patients who seek psychotherapy in outpatient clinics can be included in RCTs.

the vast majority of patients with anxiety and mood disorders who seek treatment in outpatient mental health settings are likely to be eligible for at least one published randomized controlled trial (RCT).

the vast majority of patients in the general clinical population are eligible for the psychotherapy treatments that have been studied in randomized controlled trials (i.e., cognitive-behavioral therapy [CBT], interpersonal psychotherapy, psychodynamic psychotherapy, and supportive psychotherapy), with the exception of patients with substance use disorders and patients with social anxiety disorder.
